data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference is defensible only if we accept a 'methodological falsificationism' where the rule to prefer corroborated theories is a convention, not a truth-claim.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the convention itself requires an inductive justification to be adopted.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If scientists believe they are acting on truth, not following a convention.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the convention fails to distinguish science from other rule-bound games that don't yield truth.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is 'conventionalist decree'. Popper's system survives by positing that the scientific community agrees to a set of methodological rules. One such rule is: 'Act as if the best-tested theory is the most reliable.' This is not a claim about the world (induction) nor a logical derivation, but a constitutive rule of the game of science. It is defensible on Popper's terms because it explicitly rejects the need for inductive justification, substituting it with a pragmatic agreement to facilitate progress. The cost is that the foundation of scientific action becomes arbitrary (though useful) rather than grounded in reality.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
